{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-wa-s","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"928afee4816772059f080cbfdb0cd4a23b97eac0e3921e0a8a7f6cc4e8e1d87f","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-wa-class-std:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"9f6e1cb1188348b60e3a496c6f0991207e113d4c5c50fdea6643147e46e0832e","source_liveness_sha256":"13f9e69569c91234713e9bc57e8dbd507c97dcbcafbf4df2d8e9ff3a33c56e92"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sharing the road","heading":"C — Sharing the road with people, buses, large vehicles, motorcycles, bicycles, trains and emergency vehicles","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Sharing the road with people, buses, large vehicles, motorcycles, bicycles, trains and emergency vehicles

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A93
Courtesy, respect and awareness of others are the key to sharing Washington roads, and your care could save a life, including your own. [A93]
Source: [A93 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A93
Always yield to pedestrians, who, like bicyclists, hold the right-of-way at every crosswalk and intersection, marked or unmarked. [A93]
Why it matters: an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection still gives walkers the right-of-way.
Source: [A93 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A93
Wait until a pedestrian has cleared your lane plus one more lane before going, but for someone crossing with a wheelchair, a cane, a guide dog or another service animal, stay stopped until the whole street is crossed. [A93]
Source: [A93 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A94
Watch for people who cannot see you, are distracted, or may be confused, such as children, road workers, tourists or someone on a phone. [A94]
Source: [A94 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A94
Interfering with a service animal is unlawful, and you should not honk near one because the noise can confuse or frighten the animal or its handler. [A94]
Source: [A94 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A94
School bus lights work like traffic signals: red means stop, and yellow means use caution and slow down. [A94]
Source: [A94 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A95
Passing a stopped school bus doubles the fine, and it is unlawful to pass a bus while its red lights flash. [A95]
Source: [A95 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A95
Every driver going the same direction as the bus must stop for flashing red lights and the extended stop sign, including drivers in any turn lane, and a center turn lane may never be used to pass. [A95]
Source: [A95 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A95
You may move again only once the lights stop flashing, the stop sign folds back and the metal arm returns to the front bumper, and you should keep watching for children afterward. [A95]
Source: [A95 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A96
On a 2-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop when the bus's red lights flash and its stop sign is out. [A96]
Source: [A96 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A97
On a multilane road, drivers behind the bus always stop, while the guide's exception for oncoming drivers names two conditions, a road of three or more lanes and lanes split by a median or barrier, without saying whether one alone is enough. [A97]
Why it matters: this is the main exception to stopping for a school bus, and it applies only to traffic coming the other way.
Source: [A97 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A98
Yield to a transit bus going your direction that has signaled and is pulling back into traffic. [A98]
Source: [A98 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A98
Large trucks and buses have blind zones on each side, so do not ride alongside them for long, and if you cannot see the driver's mirrors the driver cannot see you. [A98]
Source: [A98 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A98
A loaded truck with good brakes at 55 mph needs 450 feet to stop completely, so cutting in front of one without room is dangerous. [A98]
Source: [A98 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A99
Before merging in front of a large vehicle, wait until both of its headlights show in your rearview mirror, then keep up with traffic. [A99]
Source: [A99 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A99
Large vehicles may need more than one lane to turn and 2 lanes in a roundabout, and passing one while it turns is a frequent cause of crashes, so wait until the turn is done. [A99]
Source: [A99 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A99
Keep away from vehicles placarded as carrying hazardous materials when you can, and expect slow large vehicles in the right lane on long, steep grades. [A99]
Source: [A99 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A100
Snowplows can throw snow up and off the road in a blizzard-like cloud, so do not follow them closely. [A100]
Source: [A100 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A100
Motorcyclists share the same rights and traffic laws as other drivers, but they are smaller, harder to see and more vulnerable, so leave extra following room, more still on wet or slick roads. [A100]
Source: [A100 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A101
A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane width, so never move into its lane beside it, even if the rider is far to one side. [A101]
Source: [A101 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A101
Motorcycles hide easily in blind zones, so before a right turn look left, right and left again with a shoulder check, and remember drivers often misjudge an oncoming motorcycle's speed. [A101]
Source: [A101 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A101
Gravel, debris, pavement seams, potholes and even manhole covers can force a rider to change speed or lane position, so expect those moves. [A101]
Source: [A101 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A102
Riders may slow by easing the throttle without showing a brake light, and some motorcycle turn signals do not cancel on their own, so stay alert beside them. [A102]
Source: [A102 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A102
Bicyclists carry the same rights and duties as vehicle drivers, and because bikes are small and hard to see, riders face a high risk of serious injury or death. [A102]
Source: [A102 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0102]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A103
A bicyclist may legally use the full lane, you may not share a lane with one, and when following a bicyclist you leave at least 3 feet of space. [A103]
Source: [A103 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A103
A bicyclist riding in a crosswalk counts as a pedestrian, so you must yield in marked and unmarked crosswalks alike. [A103]
Source: [A103 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A103
To pass a bicyclist, move over a full lane when two lanes run your way, or use the other lane only without oncoming traffic, pass slowly on their left with at least 3 feet from your widest point, and do not pass just before a right turn. [A103]
Why it matters: the gap is measured from the widest part of your vehicle, such as a mirror.
Source: [A103 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0103]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A104
Bike lanes are often green with solid white lines and a bicycle symbol, and you may drive in one only to turn or to cross it to park at the curb. [A104]
Source: [A104 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A104
Cross railroad tracks only at designated crossings, and flashing red lights there mean a train is coming and you must stay outside the gates. [A104]
Source: [A104 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0104]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A105
Trains always have the right-of-way and can need up to a mile to stop, so stop for flashing lights and bells even if the gate is up, and never go around a gate. [A105]
Source: [A105 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A105
Stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail when signals flash, a gate is lowering or down, a flagger signals, a train is close or sounds its horn, or a stop sign is posted. [A105]
Why it matters: the stop zone has both a minimum and a maximum distance from the rail.
Source: [A105 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A105
Never stop on the tracks, and if your vehicle stalls at a crossing, get everyone out right away, because trains can come from either direction on any track. [A105]
Source: [A105 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0105]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A106
If something is on or near the tracks, phone the number shown on the crossing's blue and white Emergency Notification System sign, quote the crossing ID, or dial 911 if there is no sign. [A106]
Source: [A106 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A106
Near light rail, keep at least one car length between you and the train and never stop or park on the tracks. [A106]
Source: [A106 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A106
Farm vehicles built for 25 mph or less display a triangle emblem on the back, and passing one calls for patience, a full lane change where possible and at least 3 feet of clearance. [A106]
Source: [A106 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A107
For a fire truck, ambulance or police car using lights or sirens, pull right and stop at once, then signal and rejoin traffic only after it passes, in the order you were in before. [A107]
Source: [A107 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0107]

Glossary: right-of-way — the legal priority to go first [A93]. Slow moving vehicle emblem — the triangle on the back of a farm vehicle [A106]. Emergency Notification System sign — the blue and white sign at a rail crossing with a number to call [A106]. Bike lane — a lane marked for bicycles, often green [A104].
Memory aid: for a turning-right check near motorcycles, look left, right, left, because looking twice can save a life [A101].
